strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant gap: SAM3's noun-phrase-only concept prompting cannot handle rich, multi-condition natural-language instructions, and the paper's taxonomy (concept/simple/complex) is a clean and sensible framing of this problem space.

The cascaded adapter design (S-Adapter for simple referring expressions, C-Adapter building on it for complex/implicit reasoning) with a frozen SAM3 backbone is a parameter-efficient approach that plausibly avoids catastrophic forgetting of concept-level grounding, and this claim is at least partially supported by the reported preservation of SAM3's concept-level scores.

The instruct-mask distribution alignment loss (KL divergence) and uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision are reasonable, well-motivated auxiliary objectives, and the ablation study convincingly shows each component (curriculum stages, alignment loss, hard-region loss) contributes positively to performance.

The three-stage semi-automatic data construction pipeline (MLLM annotation, agentic quality inspection with 100%-accuracy acceptance criterion, human-in-the-loop correction for long-tail failures) is a thoughtful and scalable strategy for producing instruction-mask pairs from existing segmentation datasets.
The paper commits to open-sourcing code, model weights, and fine-tuning workflows, and reports parameter counts/inference-mode differences, supporting reproducibility and practical adoption.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly states results are 'preliminary' and that 'comprehensive evaluation is ongoing,' which is a direct admission that the work is not yet complete; this undermines confidence in the central empirical claims and is atypical for a submission expected to stand on its own evidence.

All quantitative evaluation is conducted solely on a single benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) that the authors themselves constructed using the same MLLM-based pipeline used for training data; there is no evaluation on established, independent referring/reasoning segmentation benchmarks (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, gRefCOCO, ReasonSeg) despite these being the standard comparison points for instruction-following segmentation and being mentioned as future work in the Discussion. This raises concerns about circularity and limits generalizability claims.

The comparison between SAM3-I and the SAM3+Agent baselines is confounded: SAM3-I is directly fine-tuned on the same distribution as the test set (PACO-LVIS-Instruct train split), while the agent baselines are used zero-shot with no adaptation to this benchmark or data distribution. This makes the reported gains (e.g., +12.4 gIoU) not a fair or convincing demonstration of architectural superiority versus simply the effect of in-domain fine-tuning.

No comparison against any prior reasoning-segmentation or referring-segmentation methods from the broader literature (e.g., LISA, which is even cited), making it hard to contextualize whether SAM3-I's absolute performance is competitive or merely internally consistent.

Key details on data quality and scale are missing: the proportion of instructions requiring human correction, agreement/quality metrics for the annotation-inspection loop, and potential biases introduced by using the same MLLM family (Qwen3-VL) for both data generation and the agent baseline are not reported, making it difficult to assess dataset reliability or fairness of comparisons.

The paper only evaluates on object/part-level instances from a single dataset domain (PACO-LVIS) with an N-to-1 instruction-instance structure, and the authors themselves acknowledge (in Discussion) that multi-instance/group reasoning and broader domain generalization are unaddressed, limiting the claimed scope of 'unifying concept and instruction-level reasoning within the SAM family.'

No error bars, statistical significance testing, or analysis of variance across runs/splits is provided given the relatively small effect sizes in some ablations (e.g., distribution alignment loss contributing ~1.6 gIoU).

strengths: Identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap in SAM3's promptable concept segmentation (PCS) paradigm, namely its inability to directly consume rich, multi-condition natural language instructions, and the practical downsides (overhead, information loss) of the current agentic workaround.

The proposed instruction taxonomy (concept/simple/complex) and the cascaded S-Adapter/C-Adapter design with a matched multi-stage curriculum is a coherent, well-motivated architectural story that mirrors the linguistic complexity hierarchy.

The parameter-efficient, frozen-backbone adaptation strategy is sensible for preserving SAM3's original concept-grounding ability while adding new capability, and the ablations (removing curriculum stages, alignment loss, uncertainty-aware loss) are internally consistent and show each component contributes positively on the authors' own test set.

The data construction pipeline (MLLM annotation + MLLM inspection + human correction, with explicit negative instructions as contrastive distractors) is a reasonable template for scaling instruction-mask supervision, and is described in enough procedural detail to be followed.
Writing and figures are clear, and the paper is transparent about its own limitations and future directions (Section 7), which aids interpretability of the claims.
weaknesses: The authors explicitly label the results as 'Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing' (footnote, Sec. 6) -- i.e., the paper itself states the evaluation is unfinished. This is a direct admission that the central empirical claims are not yet fully substantiated, which undermines the soundness criterion required even for a Findings recommendation.

All quantitative results are reported on a single, self-constructed benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) whose instructions, train split, and test split were generated and filtered by the same family of MLLM (Qwen3-VL) used elsewhere in the pipeline (including as the SAM3+Agent baseline component). This creates a risk of circularity/distributional match between the proposed method's training data and its own test set, and no independent, pre-existing benchmark (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, ReasonSeg, gRefCOCO) is used to validate generalization, despite ReasonSeg being explicitly deferred to 'future work.'

No comparison against established referring/reasoning segmentation baselines (e.g., LISA, PixelLM, GLaMM, or other instruction-grounded segmentation models) is provided; the only baselines are the vanilla SAM3 (which cannot do the task at all) and a self-implemented SAM3+Agent pipeline, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains represent meaningful progress relative to the broader literature.

The margin over the much larger SAM3+Agent(8.8B) baseline on complex instructions is modest (51.0 vs. 48.2 gIoU), undercutting the paper's framing of a clearly superior unified solution, especially since efficiency claims are not accompanied by actual latency/throughput measurements.

No variance/error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported; all numbers appear to be single-run point estimates, limiting confidence in the reported deltas, especially the ablation deltas which are sometimes small (e.g., 0.4-0.6 gIoU for the alignment loss).

The dataset is derived entirely from PACO-LVIS (object/part-centric, N-to-1 instance mapping), and the authors themselves note this introduces structural bias (no multi-instance/group grounding, limited domain diversity), which further restricts the generality of the 'real-world instruction' claims made in the introduction and abstract.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: while code is claimed to be open-sourced, the extensive data-generation pipeline depends on proprietary-scale compute (32 H100 GPUs for data generation, 16 for training) and a closed-source-adjacent MLLM, making independent verification costly and dependent on exact MLLM versions that may drift over time.

The paper builds directly on SAM3, which is itself an unpublished, very recent arXiv preprint (Nov 2025) without established peer review or long-term stability of released artifacts, adding downstream risk to the reproducibility and comparability of this work.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely gap: extending SAM3's promptable concept segmentation (short NP prompts) to richer, instruction-level grounding, avoiding the overhead and information loss of an external MLLM-agent pipeline that collapses complex instructions into coarse NPs.

The proposed instruction-aware cascaded adapter (S-Adapter/C-Adapter) with a matching curriculum (simple-instruction, then complex-instruction, then joint alignment) is a reasonably principled design that mirrors the natural hierarchy of linguistic complexity, and the frozen-backbone parameter-efficient adaptation strategy is sensible for preserving SAM3's original concept-driven capability.

The three-stage (annotation, inspection, human correction) data construction pipeline for producing instruction-mask pairs is a useful and reasonably scalable contribution that could benefit follow-up work even independent of the specific model.

Ablations (Table 2) cleanly isolate the contribution of curriculum stages, the distribution-alignment loss, and the uncertainty-aware hard-region loss, each showing a measurable and directionally sensible degradation when removed.

SAM3-I retains SAM3's original concept-level scores exactly (48.9/54.1), supporting the claim that the extension does not sacrifice the base model's original capability, and it does so with a single-pass, lower-parameter pipeline relative to the multi-call agent baselines.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly labels its results as 'Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing' and states 'the current version should be regarded as an initial feasibility study' -- this self-characterization, combined with the evidence provided, suggests the work is not yet mature enough for a full main-conference contribution claim.

All quantitative evaluation is confined to a single self-constructed benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) derived from the authors' own data pipeline; there is no evaluation on any established/independent referring or reasoning segmentation benchmark (e.g., RefCOCO/g/+, ReasonSeg, gRefCOCO), so generalization beyond the in-distribution, self-generated test set is unverified. The paper even lists fine-tuning/evaluating on ReasonSeg as unrealized future work.

No comparison to any existing referring/reasoning segmentation methods (e.g., LISA, PixelLM, GLaMM) is provided -- only to a same-backbone SAM3+agent baseline of the authors' own construction, limiting the ability to judge whether SAM3-I's gains represent a meaningful advance over the broader literature.

The evaluation setup appears potentially favorable to SAM3-I: it is fine-tuned and evaluated on the same PACO-LVIS-Instruct distribution it was built on, whereas the SAM3+Agent baselines are used zero-shot; this asymmetry is not discussed or controlled for.

The gains on complex instructions (the harder and more novel setting the paper emphasizes) are notably modest relative to the strongest agent baseline (51.0 vs 48.2 gIoU with Qwen3-VL-8B agent), suggesting the core reasoning capability the paper targets is only marginally improved despite the added architectural and training complexity.

No statistics on the data pipeline's yield/failure rate are reported (e.g., fraction requiring human correction, inter-annotator agreement, inspector pass rate across rounds), leaving the quality and reliability of the constructed dataset largely unverified beyond qualitative claims.

No error bars, multiple-seed results, or significance testing are reported for any of the numbers in Tables 1-2, making it hard to assess whether the reported differences (some fairly small, e.g., 0.4-0.7 gIoU in some ablations) are robust.

Reproducibility is constrained: hyperparameters are only described as following default SAM3 settings 'without modification,' with no further training details (learning rates, adapter dimensions, number of steps per stage) provided.

The paper builds entirely on a very recent, large SAM3 base model and existing dataset (PACO-LVIS), and the contribution is essentially an adapter/curriculum extension plus a data pipeline; overall technical novelty is incremental relative to the SAM3 base model and existing adapter/curriculum-learning literature.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical limitation of SAM3 (its restriction to short NP prompts and heavy reliance on an external MLLM agent pipeline) with a well-motivated, parameter-efficient solution (frozen backbone + cascaded S-/C-Adapters).

The proposed alignment losses (instruction contrastive, parent-rank concept anchoring, mask distribution alignment, uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision) are individually well-justified and their contributions are validated through a thorough ablation study (Table 5), including single- vs. multi-stage training and single- vs. cascaded-adapter comparisons.

HMPL-Instruct is a carefully constructed dataset with a documented four-stage human-in-the-loop pipeline (automatic annotation, agentic inspection, human correction, dedicated tool for one-to-many subset annotation), and the paper provides good transparency via appendix diagrams, dataset statistics, and qualitative examples.

Empirical results are consistent and favorable across multiple settings: comparison with SAM3/SAM3 Agent, evaluation across instruction complexity levels (concept/simple/complex) and target cardinalities (one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all), object vs. part granularity, and generalization to external benchmarks (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM) against strong baselines (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA).
Reasonable hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (ρ, m) and detailed implementation/reproducibility information (adapter dimensions, compute budget, training curriculum) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The work is built directly on SAM3 (Carion et al., 2025), an extremely recent (essentially concurrent) and reportedly proprietary-leaning foundation model; this dependency raises concerns about external reproducibility and verifiability by readers who cannot access or fully evaluate the SAM3 backbone independently of this paper's claims.

The technical contribution is somewhat incremental — a bottleneck adapter + auxiliary alignment losses inserted into an existing frozen backbone — rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea; the core novelty largely rests on the specific combination of losses and the curated dataset rather than a new architectural or theoretical insight.

Dataset quality claims rely on an automatic MLLM annotation/inspection loop (same/similar underlying MLLM family, Qwen3-VL, used both for generation and inspection and possibly as a baseline agent), which could introduce self-consistency bias; no quantitative statistics are reported on inter-annotator agreement, rejection/correction rates, or human-verified accuracy of the final dataset beyond qualitative description.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonable given the novelty of the setting, are limited in number (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA, and a single SAM3-Agent configuration using one MLLM, Qwen3-VL-8B); it is unclear how sensitive the SAM3-Agent baseline's performance is to the choice or scale of the external MLLM, which affects the strength of the 'preserves efficiency while beating agent pipelines' claim.

The paper's own Limitations section acknowledges the one-to-many setting remains comparatively underexplored and data-imbalanced, and the framework does not extend to deeper semantic/conversational reasoning, which somewhat tempers the scope of the claimed contribution.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and timely problem: extending SAM3's concept-level promptable segmentation to handle richer natural-language instructions without relying on an external multi-modal agent pipeline, which is a reasonable and practically relevant research question.

The proposed instruction-aware cascaded adapter (S-Adapter/C-Adapter) with a battery of alignment losses (instruction contrastive loss, parent-rank concept anchoring loss, mask distribution KL alignment, uncertainty-aware hard-region loss) is clearly described and is accompanied by a fairly thorough ablation study (Table 5, hyperparameter sweeps for ρ and m) that isolates the contribution of each component and the multi-stage curriculum.

The HMPL-Instruct dataset construction pipeline is clearly documented (automatic annotation, agentic quality inspection, human-in-the-loop correction, dedicated annotation tool for one-to-many cases) and the released dataset statistics (133,960 object masks, 213,160 part masks, 849,792 instructions) suggest a reasonably large-scale resource.

Experiments span multiple evaluation settings (concept/simple/complex instructions, one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all cardinalities, object- and part-level granularity) plus external benchmarks (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM), giving a reasonably broad empirical picture.

The paper is clearly written with a logical structure, good figures illustrating the pipeline differences from SAM3/SAM3 Agent, and an extensive appendix with implementation details, qualitative examples, and ethics/artifact statements.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evidence (Tables 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) is almost entirely measured on the authors' own HMPL-Instruct benchmark, which was itself generated and verified largely by the same family of MLLM (Qwen3-VL) that is also used to build the SAM3-Agent baseline being compared against; this creates a risk of circularity/bias in favor of the proposed method and the paper reports no independent human-agreement or dataset-quality statistics (e.g., inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates per stage, measured annotation noise) to substantiate the claimed instruction-grounding quality.

On the one external, independently-constructed and widely used benchmark (RefCOCO), SAM3-I does not actually outperform the existing non-agent method UniPixel (76.3/80.0 gIoU/P@50 for SAM3-I vs. 78.1/84.4 for UniPixel), undercutting the paper's central claim of superior instruction-following performance; the Ref-ZOM comparison is more favorable but the mixed results across the two standard benchmarks weaken the overall evidentiary strength.

The method is built entirely on top of SAM3 (Carion et al., 2025), a contemporaneous/very recent arXiv preprint whose code, weights, and licensing status are not clearly verifiable at the time of this submission; this raises concerns about independent reproducibility of the baseline and the proposed extension beyond what the authors themselves can demonstrate.

Performance on complex, NP-free instructions remains substantially and consistently lower than on simple instructions across all tables (e.g., 59.7/65.3 simple vs. 49.0/51.0 complex gIoU/P@50 in Table 2), indicating that the core challenge the paper aims to address (implicit/functional/relational reasoning) is only partially solved, yet this gap is not critically discussed as a limitation of the core contribution.

The technical contribution is a fairly incremental combination of well-established techniques (bottleneck adapters, InfoNCE-style contrastive loss, margin ranking loss, KL-divergence distribution matching, uncertainty-weighted cross-entropy) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty mainly lies in dataset curation and task formulation rather than methodological innovation.

The most challenging and arguably most interesting one-to-many setting is acknowledged to rely entirely on manual, non-scalable human annotation (Stage 4), which is in tension with the paper's claims of a "scalable" instruction-centric data engine and limits the generality of the released dataset for that setting.

No human evaluation or qualitative comparison with independent/human judges is provided beyond a handful of cherry-picked qualitative examples (Fig. 4, Fig. 8), making it harder to assess real-world grounding quality beyond the automatic gIoU/P@50 metrics on the self-constructed benchmark.

strengths: Addresses a clear, well-motivated gap: SAM3's agent-based pipeline for handling complex natural-language instructions is coarse (collapses to short NPs) and computationally expensive; SAM3-I removes the external MLLM loop and directly grounds instructions.

Technically well-designed instruction-aware cascaded adapter (S-Adapter/C-Adapter) with four complementary alignment losses (instruction contrastive, parent-rank concept anchoring, mask distribution KL, uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision), each ablated individually with sensible, interpretable results in Table 5.

Parameter-efficient design keeps the SAM3 backbone frozen (~0.3B added parameters) and empirically preserves original concept-level (PCS) performance, avoiding catastrophic forgetting while adding new capability.

New HMPL-Instruct dataset fills a real gap in the benchmark landscape by unifying concept/simple/complex instruction levels, object/part granularity, and one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all target cardinalities in a single resource (Table 1 comparison is informative).

Human-in-the-loop data construction pipeline (automatic annotation, agentic inspection, human correction, dedicated dual-panel tool for one-to-many subset selection) is described with good reproducibility detail, including annotator/inspector protocol.

Strong empirical results: outperforms SAM3 Agent (Qwen3-VL-8B) and other reasoning-segmentation baselines (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA) on HMPL-Instruct, RefCOCO, and Ref-ZOM while using a single-pass, smaller-parameter pipeline; ablations on multi-stage curriculum and cascaded vs. single adapter support key design choices.
Reasonable implementation/reproducibility details (hyperparameters, training compute, adapter architecture) and code/dataset release promised.
weaknesses: The training data (HMPL-Instruct) and the primary agent baseline (SAM3 Agent) both rely on the same MLLM family (Qwen3-VL), which raises a potential fairness/circularity concern: SAM3-I is effectively distilled from Qwen3-VL-generated/verified instructions, so part of its advantage over the Qwen3-VL-based agent baseline may reflect this asymmetry rather than purely architectural gains; the paper does not test agent baselines with a different/larger MLLM to control for this.

One-to-many instruction-instance data is obtained through a separate, purely human-driven annotation stage (Stage 4) that is acknowledged as limited in scale/diversity; the paper's own Limitations section flags this data imbalance, which constrains claims about the model's general subset-level/group reasoning ability.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonable (LISA, UniPixel, ReLA, SAM3 Agent), are not exhaustive relative to the fast-moving reasoning-segmentation literature, and no results are shown for stronger/larger agent MLLMs, alternative segmentation backbones, or robustness to paraphrased/adversarial instructions.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for the main quantitative results, and dataset quality is validated mainly via MLLM-based 100%-consistency filtering plus limited human correction rather than an independent human quality/agreement study.

The dataset is derived from a single source (PACO-LVIS), limiting domain diversity; scaling to more diverse imagery is left as future work, so generalization beyond this benchmark's visual/instruction distribution is untested.

Method and dataset novelty, while solid engineering contributions, are largely combinatorial (known techniques: bottleneck adapters, contrastive/margin losses, KL alignment, curriculum training) applied to a new setting; the core insight is incremental relative to SAM3 and existing reasoning-segmentation work rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.
